title.$t: Phantom Arcades: +92% search clicks in 68 days

content.$t:
Google sent Phantom Arcades 2,130 clicks in the 68 days after we took over its search, up from 1,112 in the same 68 days a year earlier (+92%). Every number below is from the site's own Google Search Console, matched to the same calendar dates so the season cancels out.

Why it matters: Phantom Arcades hand-builds every machine to order in Valrico, Florida ($1,999 to $14,999, shipped across the lower 48). There is no product shelf to rank, only a builder people have to find. The searches that do not include the brand name, the ones search work earns, went from 95 to 314 clicks (+231%).

By the numbers

Search Console property totals, not summed query rows (those undercount).

Same 68 daysClicksImpressionsNon-brand clicksNon-brand impressions
Aug 13 – Oct 19, 20251,11231,9789511,172
Aug 13 – Oct 19, 20262,13052,22631417,366
Change+92%+63%+231%+55%
  • The control: the 68 days before we started (June 6 to August 12, 2026 against 2025) were flat: clicks −6%, impressions +3%.
  • Week by week: ahead of the same week last year in 9 of 10 weeks. The exception was the week of September 17 (217 against 226).
  • Month by month, 2026: July 437 · August 744 · September 1,016.
  • Why non-brand leads: brand searches move with press, social posts and word of mouth. A search for "custom arcade cabinet" or "Sega Naomi games" that finds Phantom is the part search work earns.

What we changed

  • Rebuilt the site so Google could read it. Fast static pages replaced the old WordPress site. More than 80 permanent redirects, each checked against a live target, carried the old links and rankings over.
  • Built pages for what people actually search. One page per game system (up to 50 systems, thousands of games), listing the titles and the cabinets that run them. About half of non-brand impressions now land there: Sega Model 3, Naomi, Wii light-gun searches finding a builder who puts those games in a cabinet.
  • Made every product page say what it is. Titles name the machine the way buyers search ("4-player arcade cabinet", "hidden arcade cabinet"). The HideAway ranks in Google's top three for "hideaway arcade" and around fifth for "hidden arcade cabinet".
  • Added structured product data (price, availability, shipping by region) so search engines can show the machines as products.
  • Fixed what visitors showed us without saying it. Microsoft Clarity showed half of phone visitors leaving before 15% of the homepage; the first phone screen opened on about 66 pixels of empty space above the video. Removing it put the first machine and its price on the first screen. Clarity also caught the 3D designer throwing an error when buyers switched cabinets quickly; that is fixed in the code and we are watching the error data to confirm it.

What we can measure now

Phantom had no web analytics and no Bing account before September, so these numbers have no year-earlier comparison. They show where buyers come from and what they do.

  • Bing (Webmaster Tools, September 13 to October 18): 2,399 impressions, 54 clicks. Bing also feeds the web answers in Copilot and ChatGPT.
  • Google Analytics 4 (installed September 9, figures to October 19), sessions by source:
Where visits came fromSessions
Social media3,465
Direct (typed, bookmarks, links in messages)2,777
Organic search2,128
Other websites110
AI assistants (ChatGPT, Copilot, Perplexity and similar)106
  • In the 3D configurator over the same period: 1,995 designs started, 157 full builds finished, 471 checkouts opened, 15 enquiries sent through the site's forms.

AI search

Buyers now ask ChatGPT, Google's AI Overview and Perplexity "who makes the best custom arcade machines". We measured two things: whether the answers name Phantom, and whether they send visitors.

  • Visits from AI assistants (GA4, September 9 to October 19): 106 sessions. 66% were engaged, the second-best rate of any channel after email (organic social 58%, direct 30%). Average stay 137 seconds, 12 to 25 visits a week, landing on the home page, the 3D designer, the Multicade and the Phantom Evolution pages. They produced 2 of the site's key events.
AI sourceSessionsEngaged
ChatGPT10369
Gemini20
Copilot11
  • Whether AI answers name Phantom (our test, October 6, fresh logged-out sessions, each question repeated because answers change run to run): Google AI Overview named Phantom on 9 of 10 buyer wordings, including "best custom arcade machine makers" and "under $3000". ChatGPT named Phantom #1 on every Florida, Tampa and Valrico question (7 of 7) and #1 or #2 on all 3 runs of "who makes the best custom arcade machines in the USA, and what do they cost", because Phantom publishes its prices. Four more models with web search (Grok, Claude, GPT mini, Gemini; 96 answers) named Phantom first for "custom arcade builders Florida" on every run, and cited phantomarcades.com 39 times, ahead of every competitor (the next: 27).
  • Where AI still misses: the plain "best in the USA" question (ChatGPT 0 of 3 runs) and budget questions ("under $3000"). Our response, published October 6: a pricing-page section listing the models under $3,000 and answering those questions directly. We will re-run the same test and report it here.
  • Why AI favours Phantom where it does: the site states facts an AI can quote, namely prices, where it is built and what is in each machine. Pages with real prices and specifics get cited. Pages of adjectives don't.

What's next

  • Clicks lag impressions. Google shows the site far more often; the click-through rate on the main commercial phrase is still low.
  • The money phrase is on page 2. The homepage ranks 11th to 18th for "custom arcade machines" and "custom arcade cabinet". Moving it to page one is mostly authority: the builders above it have far more reviews (one shows 450+) and stronger links.
  • No revenue claim yet. Every Phantom machine takes 12 to 16 weeks to build, so sales from this traffic land months after the click. We report revenue when the order book shows it. Next measurement: November, in this post.

The bottom line

  • Measure against the same dates last year, and show the period before you started. Without the control, a seasonal rise looks like your work.
  • Report property totals. Summing Search Console's query table drops every rare query Google hides for privacy.
  • The long tail is real demand. Nobody searching for a Sega Naomi game list is a tire-kicker.

Go deeper: the site's 3D configurator was built first; that work is in our product configurator case study. If you build something to order and need people to find you, see how we run SEO.

title.$t: Build it, price it, send it: what a product configurator is actually for

content.$t:
Short version: a 3D product configurator is not a toy on a product page. Its job is to turn a browsing session into a written specification the business can quote from. If it does not do that, it is an expensive spinning object.

The client

Phantom Arcades hand-builds custom arcade cabinets in Valrico, Florida. Dennis Riese builds them one at a time, to order. Nothing about that business fits a normal product page, because there is no product to put on it. There is a range of machines, and then there is whatever a customer asks for.

That is the actual design problem. Not "show the products". Let someone describe a machine that does not exist yet, and get a number back.

Eight cabinets, one interface, $1,999 to $14,999

The site configures eight machines. They are not variants of each other.

The HideAway Arcade is $1,999 and its whole point is disappearing. The hood closes over the controls and it stops looking like an arcade machine, which is how it gets into a living room instead of a basement. In the configurator it actually closes, because a still photograph cannot explain a thing that transforms.

The Final Boss is $14,999 and is the opposite argument. Four players, 53 by 34 by 78 inches, three screens running at once, guitars and a drum pedal. It is furniture that dominates a room on purpose.

In between sit the Retro Revival at $2,199, three sizes of Level Up from $2,799 to $3,999, the Phantom Evolution at $3,700, and a portable case.

Here is the part worth stealing: the same three controls sit under every one of them. Save link. Build sheet. And then the enquiry, which is the only one that changes wording by machine — "Reserve build slot" on the ones with a list price, "Call to spec yours" on the Final Boss, which is a conversation rather than an order. A customer who has never seen an arcade cabinet does not have to learn a second interface to price the expensive one.

These are his machines, not our approximation of them

Every cabinet in that configurator except the portable case is loaded from Dennis's own SolidWorks export. Nine model files, prepped and optimised, but the geometry is his.

We started out drawing our own version of his product. It was wrong in the way approximations always are: near-enough silhouette, deck at the wrong height, buttons in roughly the right place. We threw it away. There is no reason to approximate a thing you have been given.

This is the least glamorous decision on the project and probably the most important one. A customer who has seen the real machine will recognise a fake, and the moment they do, every other number on the page becomes a claim rather than a fact.

The 3D is not the achievement

Rotating a cabinet is impressive for about eight seconds. Then it is wallpaper.

What the 3D actually buys you is that people change things. They try the four player deck. They price the next tier of internals. They see what $2,500 of upgrades looks like before deciding they do not want it. The model is a reason to keep touching the page, and touching the page is how someone arrives at a specification instead of a vague interest.

The mistake is to stop there. Most configurators do. You build the machine, you admire it, and the page offers you nothing but a contact form that has no idea what you just spent twenty minutes doing.

The three buttons that do the work

Save link. The whole build encodes into a URL. Send it to a partner, reopen it next week, paste it into an email to Dennis. Nothing is lost between the evening someone spent choosing and the morning they decide.

Build sheet. A plain text summary of exactly what was selected, with the price and the artwork notes. Not a PDF that needs a viewer. Something a person can paste into a message and a builder can read without opening the site.

The enquiry. It arrives already knowing the machine, the options and the number. Dennis is not starting from "hi, how much is an arcade machine".

That is the actual handoff, and it is the reason the configurator pays for itself. The 3D gets attention. The build sheet turns attention into something quotable.

Pricing in the open

The price moves as you choose: the machine, the internals, the button package, the sound, the controls. Custom artwork is a line item, not a conversation.

Showing the number is a commercial decision, not a technical one, and plenty of custom builders refuse to. The argument for showing it is that "call for pricing" filters out the people who would have bought and keeps the people who were never going to. A $14,999 machine should say $14,999 on the page. The people it scares off were not customers.

What is not finished

The configurator page is slow. It scores 34 out of 100 on a mobile performance test, and on a mid-range phone the browser is unresponsive for around seven seconds while it builds the 3D scene. Three.js and the model loading account for about six and a half of those seconds.

We know the fix, and we have not shipped it yet. The geometry is being assembled in the browser on every single visit when almost all of it could be baked once at build time and downloaded ready to draw.

We did do this work elsewhere on the site, so the approach is proven rather than theoretical. The Arcade 101 page took 7.8 seconds to show its main content on a phone and locked the browser for 3.3 seconds. It now shows in about 3.6 seconds with 1.9 seconds of blocking, and no image or video on the page was degraded to get there.

Saying this out loud is deliberate. An agency case study that reports only wins is not describing a real project.

Four questions before you commission one of these

What does someone leave with? If the answer is "an impression", the 3D is decoration. They should leave with a link, a sheet, or an enquiry that already contains the build.

Is the geometry real? Ask whether it is the manufacturer's model or an artist's version of it. On a made-to-order product, the difference is credibility.

Does the price show? If it does not, be honest that the tool is a lead filter rather than a sales tool, and design it as one.

What does a search engine see? Ours currently sees an estimated total of $0, because the price is calculated in the browser and a crawler does not run it. That is on the list with the performance work.

What Dennis said

He left this on our Google listing after the site went live. His words, unedited.

D
Dennis Riese
★★★★★ Phantom Arcades · Valrico, FL

Lou is an absolute pleasure to work with. From the moment we started working together till when my website went live, Lou has helped me every step of the way. I have never worked with someone so knowledgeable about what product they offer. I recommend OneAlgorithm but if you do reach out to them make sure you ask for Lou!

Posted on Google · Read it on our Google listing

He is also, obviously, not a neutral party — he paid for the work. Read it as a client saying the process was worth it, not as evidence that the site performs. The numbers earlier in this post are the evidence.

The point

The demanding part of this build was never the 3D. Three.js is well documented and the models were handed to us. The demanding part was deciding what a person walks away holding, and then making the page produce that thing.

Build it, price it, send it. If a configurator does not do the third one, it is a toy with a hosting bill.

OneAlgorithm designed and developed phantomarcades.com, including the eight-cabinet 3D configurator, the generated build archive and the room fit checker. We build and market websites for small businesses from Malvern, Pennsylvania.

link.title: Build it, price it, send it: what a product configurator is actually for

title.$t: Home Inspector Website Design: What Makes One Actually Bring In Work

content.$t:
Short version: Home inspector website design fails for one reason more often than any other — the site never names the towns the inspector actually covers, so it never turns up when someone in those towns goes looking. That is a structural problem, not a design one, and a prettier site does not fix it.

Home inspector website design is almost always judged on how the site looks. That is the wrong test. An inspection site earns its keep when a buyer two towns over, under contract and on a clock, searches for an inspector and finds you.

Most don't. They are built as one page with a phone number on it, or on a template that says "serving the greater metro area" — a phrase no human being has ever typed into Google. The site looks perfectly good. As far as search is concerned it does not exist.

If yours isn't sending you anything, send us the address. We will look at it and tell you plainly what is wrong.

What we changed for Lou

Lou Rubino runs Inspect This Home Inspections across Nassau and Long Island — thirty years building and renovating houses before he ever started inspecting them. The work was there. The website wasn't bringing him much of it.

We built him a new one from scratch:

  • A page for every area he covers, rather than one page claiming all of them at once
  • Online scheduling, so a buyer under contract can book at nine at night instead of waiting for a callback
  • Inspection reports he updates himself, without having to ring anyone
  • Licence and certification numbers on the page, where a nervous first-time buyer actually looks for them

In his own words, on Google:

"One algorithm did a great job on my new web site design and development… They are also directing more traffic to my site resulting in more business."

— Lou Rubino's review

Twenty-six pages covering the towns he genuinely works in went live at the end of August. That work is still going.

Why naming the towns is the whole game

A search engine can only match you to a place you have named. "Serving Long Island" does not match somebody searching for an inspector in one specific town. A real page about that town does.

None of this is unique to home inspection — it is true of every local trade — but it bites hardest here, because the buyer is on a deadline and picks from whoever shows up.

If your website isn't bringing you work

Send us the address and we will tell you what is wrong with it, and whether it is worth fixing. Some sites need rebuilding. Plenty just need three pages that do not exist yet.

We build websites for small businesses and run the search work that makes them findable, from Malvern, Pennsylvania.

title.$t: Senior Business Systems Engineer I – Malvern, PA

content.$t:
Location: Malvern, Pennsylvania

One Algorithm LLC is seeking a Senior Business Systems Engineer I to design and develop solutions to complex application problems, system administration issues, and network concerns. The successful candidate will lead initiatives to modernize infrastructure, integrate enterprise applications, and resolve mission-critical technical challenges across diverse technology environments.

Responsibilities

The Senior Business Systems Engineer I will:

  • Architect and develop application solutions using Java, C#, Python, .NET, and Node.js.
  • Design microservices and API-driven architectures using Spring Boot, RESTful APIs, and GraphQL.
  • Analyze and optimize application performance using New Relic, AppDynamics, Dynatrace, and related profiling tools.
  • Administer enterprise systems across Windows Server, Red Hat Linux, Ubuntu Linux, VMware vSphere, and Hyper-V environments.
  • Deploy and manage containerized applications using Docker, Kubernetes, and OpenShift.
  • Implement enterprise monitoring and logging solutions using Splunk, Prometheus, Grafana, and the ELK Stack.
  • Design, configure, and troubleshoot enterprise networks, including latency, bandwidth, availability, and security concerns.
  • Configure and manage Cisco, Juniper, and Palo Alto firewalls, routers, and switches.
  • Implement and support networking protocols and technologies, including TCP/IP, DNS, DHCP, VPN, SSL/TLS, and IPSec.
  • Integrate ERP, CRM, HRMS, and other enterprise applications using MuleSoft, Dell Boomi, Apache Camel, and related middleware platforms.
  • Support data integration and exchange using Informatica, Talend, and SQL Server Integration Services.
  • Develop and maintain CI/CD pipelines using Jenkins, GitLab CI, and Azure DevOps.
  • Design hybrid and cloud-native solutions using Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform.
  • Work with AWS services including EC2, RDS, and Lambda; Azure services including AKS and Azure Functions; and Google Cloud services including BigQuery and Google Kubernetes Engine.
  • Implement Infrastructure as Code using Terraform, Ansible, and AWS CloudFormation.
  • Design high-availability, disaster-recovery, backup, clustering, and load-balancing solutions.
  • Apply cybersecurity best practices, including identity and access management using Okta, Microsoft Active Directory, and LDAP.
  • Conduct vulnerability assessments and technical analysis using Nessus, Qualys, Wireshark, and related security tools.
  • Support compliance with SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR, and ISO 27001 requirements.
  • Lead cross-functional teams through requirements analysis, solution design, implementation, testing, and deployment.
  • Collaborate with business stakeholders to align technology solutions with organizational objectives.
  • Mentor junior engineers and analysts on system design, administration, integration, and implementation practices.

Required Technologies

Candidates must have experience working with:

Programming and application development: Java, Python, C#, .NET, Node.js, Spring Boot, RESTful APIs, and GraphQL.

Systems and infrastructure: Windows Server, Linux, VMware vSphere, Hyper-V, Docker, Kubernetes, and OpenShift.

Networking and security: Cisco, Juniper, Palo Alto, TCP/IP, DNS, DHCP, VPN, SSL/TLS, IPSec, Okta, Active Directory, LDAP, Nessus, Qualys, and Wireshark.

Integration and data tools: MuleSoft, Dell Boomi, Apache Camel, Informatica, Talend, and SSIS.

Cloud and DevOps: AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform, Jenkins, GitLab CI, Azure DevOps, Terraform, Ansible, and CloudFormation.

Monitoring and logging: Splunk, Prometheus, Grafana, ELK Stack, New Relic, AppDynamics, and Dynatrace.

Education and Experience

The position requires:

  • A bachelor’s degree in Computer Science, Information Systems, Engineering, or a related field.
  • Five years of experience as a software professional in systems engineering, systems administration, systems integration, or a related occupation.

Work Location and Relocation

This position is based in Malvern, Pennsylvania.

No domestic or international travel is required. The position may involve up to a 40% chance of relocation to unanticipated locations throughout the United States.

How to Apply

Qualified applicants should email their résumé to:

careers@onealgorithm.com
